questions.question: The formula for average gradient is:
options: Horizontal equivalent divided by vertical interval
Vertical interval divided by horizontal equivalent
Vertical interval multiplied by horizontal equivalent
Contour interval divided by map scale

questions.question: A gradient of 1 : 4 means that:
options: The land rises 4 metres for every 1 metre travelled horizontally
The slope covers 4 kilometres in total
The land rises 1 metre for every 4 metres travelled horizontally

questions.question: Comparing 1 : 20 with 1 : 200, the correct statement is:
options: 1 : 20 is steeper, because the metre of climb is packed into a shorter horizontal distance
1 : 200 is steeper, because 200 is the bigger number
Neither can be compared without the map scale

subtopics.title: Extracting VI and HE from the Map

questions.question: On a topographic map, a small triangle with a station number marks:
options: A trig beacon with a surveyed, exact altitude

questions.question: With beacon 89 at 1 350 m and a spot height at 1 100 m, the vertical interval is:
options: 250 metres, found by subtracting the lower height from the higher

questions.question: A measured map distance of 10 cm on a 1:50 000 sheet converts to a ground distance of:
options: 5 kilometres — 10 times 50 000 gives 500 000 cm, which is 5 000 m

questions.question: Before dividing VI by HE, you must first:
options: Express both values in the same unit, normally metres
Round both values to the nearest hundred

subtopics.title: The Calculation — Laid Out for Marks

questions.question: The four written lines of a full gradient answer are:
options: Formula, substitution with units, simplification, answer as 1 : x

questions.question: Simplifying 250 over 5 000 to the form 1 : x gives:
Presenting the final answer as 0,05 instead of 1 : 20 usually:
options: Earns a bonus mark for extra precision
Forfeits the answer mark, because the ratio form 1 : x is the required presentation
Is required when the distance was measured

questions.question: The answer is called an AVERAGE gradient because:
options: The total rise is spread evenly over the total distance, ignoring dips and climbs along the way
Several learners' answers are averaged together
The two heights are averaged before subtracting
The map scale is an average of many surveys

subtopics.title: Verification, Traps and the Full Method

questions.question: The reverse-arithmetic check for the answer 1 : 20 is:
Dividing 250 metres by 5 instead of 5 000 is the trap of:
options: Mixed units — the 5 was kilometres and was never converted to metres
Subtracting heights in the wrong order

questions.question: Writing the answer as 20 : 1 is wrong because:
options: Ratios may never contain the number 20
The colon should be a decimal point
The answer must always be rounded first
The '1' in the ratio belongs to the vertical climb, not the horizontal distance

questions.question: At 1:50 000, a measuring error of 2 millimetres on the map equals a ground error of:
options: 100 metres, which is why you measure to the nearest half millimetre

questions.question: A clinic's staircase and its wheelchair ramp both reach the same door. They differ in:
options: The horizontal distance travelled while climbing the same height
The number of people they can carry

questions.question: The single question you ask a slope to find its gradient is:
options: For every metre I go up, how many metres do I go along?
How many contour lines does it cross?
How long does it take to walk?
How high is the highest point?

questions.question: In the teaspoon-of-concentrate picture, pouring the same teaspoon into a bigger jug stands for:
options: Spreading one metre of climb across a longer walk, making the slope gentler

questions.question: The formal names for the 'up' number and the 'along' number are:

subtopics.title: Two Numbers Off the Map, Both Speaking Metres

questions.question: The climb between beacon 89 at 1 350 m and the spot height at 1 100 m is found by:
options: Taking the low height away from the high one: 1 350 minus 1 100 gives 250 metres
Multiplying the heights by the scale

questions.question: Un-shrinking 10 cm of paper distance on a 1:50 000 map means:
options: Multiplying by 50 000 to get 500 000 cm, then converting to 5 000 m

questions.question: Dividing metres of climb by kilometres of distance is compared in the lesson to:
options: Working out a price by dividing rands by cents — the answer is a thousand times out

questions.question: Before dividing, 5 kilometres must be written as:
options: 5 000 metres, so that both numbers speak metres

subtopics.title: Share It Out, Then Say It in One Line

questions.question: Sharing 5 000 among 250 is compared to:
options: Counting how many R250 concert tickets a R5 000 prize will buy — the answer is 20
Splitting a bill between two friends
Estimating a taxi fare from the distance

questions.question: Handing in the answer as 0,05 or as 250 over 5 000 is compared to:
options: Paying at a till with a jar of loose five-cent pieces — the value is there but the form is not accepted

questions.question: A slope of 1 : 20 in everyday terms is:
options: So gentle you would never notice it
Genuinely steep — a minibus changes down and a railway would not be built on it

questions.question: If the height subtraction comes out negative, you should:
options: Start the whole calculation again from the map
Keep only the size of the difference, because steepness is the same uphill and downhill
Report the gradient as a negative ratio
Swap the vertical and horizontal numbers
